[cheerful] First lesson: relational databases.

Discover how data is organized into tables and linked together.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] NutriBoost is an online store for dietary supplements.

To track its orders, the team keeps a simple Excel file.

Each row is an order: the customer, their email, the product, its price and the quantity ordered.

One column per attribute, and one row per order.

Where the two meet is a cell: the email of the customer Sophie Martin.

Each row groups information about the customer, the product bought and the order.

With every new order or request, the file gets heavier, and it becomes hard to find your way around it.

It is updated by several people, from several different teams.

And errors start to appear.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] The customer Sophie Martin ordered three times, so she takes up three rows.

So her first name, last name and email are copied three times.

The name and price of the Prebiotic Fiber are repeated with every order of this product.

If Sophie Martin changes her email, it has to be fixed on every row.

Miss one row, and the file has two emails for the same customer.

To avoid these inconsistencies, each piece of information must be stored in one single place.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] The proposed solution: split the information into three tables: customers, products and orders.

Each table groups the information about one subject.

For example, the first name, last name and email are in the customers table.

A table organizes data into rows and columns, like an Excel sheet.

The first name, last name and email go into the customers table.

The customer Sophie Martin now appears only once.

The product and its price go into the products table.

What’s left is the orders table: the identifier of each order and its quantity.

The information is now split across three tables.

Each customer and each product appears only once in its table.

It isn’t copied, even if it appears in several orders.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] What is a database?

A database is a set of organized information.

That way, you can find it and update it easily.

Here, it holds the data of our company in three tables: customers, orders and products.

It is managed by a DBMS: a database management system.

There are several, widely used: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle or SQL Server.

The NutriBoost website uses this database.

A customer opens the products page: the website then sends an SQL query to the DBMS to get them.

The DBMS runs it: it reads the products in the products table.

It sends the result back to the website, which shows it on screen.

When the customer orders, the website sends another query.

The DBMS saves the order in the orders table, and the website confirms it to the customer.
elements.avant: It isn’t copied, even if it appears in several orders.
elements.apres: SQL is the language used to communicate with the DBMS.

elements.titre: 05 · Base de données et SGBD (le SQL et la requête)
elements.texte:
[cheerful] SQL is the language used to communicate with the DBMS.

A query is an instruction written in SQL: it asks the DBMS to read or change data.

Here, select star from products asks to show all the products in our catalog (the products table).
elements.avant: The DBMS saves the order in the orders table, and the website confirms it to the customer.
elements.apres: The data is now split into tables, but a relationship between them is still missing.
phrases: SQL is the language used to communicate with the DBMS.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] The data is now split into tables, but a relationship between them is still missing.

For each order, how do you find the customer and the product, if they’re in different tables?

We add an ID column to identify each customer without any confusion.

Even if two customers have the same name, each one has their own identifier.

It’s written table dot column: customers dot ID means the ID column of the customers table.

Same thing in products dot ID: the Prebiotic Fiber has the identifier 1.

Why store the customer’s identifier in the order rather than their first name?

Two customers are named Nathan, and both live in Paris.

An order marked “Nathan” wouldn’t say which one.

The primary key never repeats: order number 5 has the identifier 4, the one of Nathan Petit.

It is declared when the table is created, with primary key placed right after the column type.

With auto increment, the DBMS generates the identifier of each new customer itself.

No need to type it in with every new row.

The DBMS rejects adding Yanis Roche with the identifier 4, already used by Nathan Petit.

For Lina Garnier, the identifier 11 is generated automatically, because the ID column was set up for it.
elements.avant: Here, select star from products asks to show all the products in our catalog (the products table).
elements.apres: Integer is the data type of the ID column: a whole number.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] To link the tables, we add two columns to the orders table: customer underscore ID and product underscore ID.

In the orders table, the customer underscore ID column holds the identifier of the customer who placed the order.

For example, the value 1 points to Sophie Martin, whose identifier is 1 in the customers table.

These identifiers, which point to the primary key of another table, are foreign keys.

In order number 1, customer underscore ID equals 1 means Sophie Martin.

Its product underscore ID equals 1 means the Prebiotic Fiber.

So we find out she ordered 2 units of it.

Sophie Martin’s three orders contain her identifier 1.

Her name and email are stored only once, in the customers table.

They aren’t copied into each order.

These identifiers link the tables: that’s what makes the database relational.

The foreign key is declared with foreign key and its column, then references and the key it points to.

The DBMS then checks each link: is there a customer with the identifier 99?

No row of customers dot ID has this identifier: the order is rejected.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] To read a table, you write select star from followed by its name.

The star selects all the columns.

From customers says which table to get the data from.

The query shows the 10 customers, one per row.

Each row holds all the information stored in the 9 columns of the table.

With select, you only look at the data.

The result is shown, but the information stored in the table stays unchanged.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] To send an email to customers, three columns are enough: the first name, the last name and the email.

Just write their names instead of the star, separated by a comma.

The columns are shown in the order you write them: first the first name, then the last name, then the email.

The result shows one row per customer, with their first name, last name and email.

Sophie Martin’s contact details are no longer repeated for each of her orders.

They are grouped in the customers table.

In an upcoming lesson, you’ll discover joins.

They let you bring together information from several tables.

That way, you’ll be able to see who ordered what, just like in our original Excel sheet.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] To select several columns, separate their names with a comma.

Don’t add one after the last one: select first underscore name, last underscore name, email.

And what if you forget the comma between first underscore name and email?

The DBMS reads email as a new title for the first underscore name column.

Result: the first names show up under the title “email”, without the email addresses.

With one comma too many before from, the query causes an error.
